title: Installing Process Control
hook: The a production board with blank score columns turns process control from a promise into work due before Friday.
counterintuition: A written plan can look like control while nothing reviews or supports it; the useful turn is to install a weekly routine that keeps commitments visible.
tryThisNow: Schedule a 20-minute weekly review for this week and invite one person who should know what you are committing to execute.
keyTakeaway: Install a weekly operating routine that turns the plan into reviewed, scheduled, socially supported action. The standard is visible action, not a better-sounding intention.

A written plan can still become a false comfort when the week never forces it to prove itself. This stage attacks that problem. The execution system move from planning into process control because execution decays unless the plan keeps returning to the week as a live operating demand. The title is precise. Installing Process Control means the missing piece is not more belief in the plan but recurring structure. Making Sure Things Get Done frames the stage as a question of control rather than a question of caring enough. Weekly Plans and The Weekly Routine carry most of the weight. The larger plan sets direction, but the weekly layer decides whether commitments become present-tense action. If weekly planning is absent, then urgency, mood, and improvisation start replacing chosen priorities. The routine keeps the plan visible often enough to resist that drift. Don't Go It Alone adds the next pressure. Private commitments are easy to reinterpret because nobody else sees the slippage in real time. Accountability matters because outside visibility exposes delay before it hardens into the new normal. It gives the plan a witness. The limit keeps the stage from turning into bureaucracy. Process control is not a defense of meetings, rituals, or calendar order as ends in themselves. It matters only when the weekly operating rhythm keeps important commitments exposed to action and prevents the system from hiding behind organized-looking activity. Thinking Shift, Team Application, and Common Pitfalls widen the lesson. The shift is from assuming a strong plan will hold to assuming it will decay without recurring exposure. Teams need the same weekly structure because shared direction is still too soft on its own. Pitfalls appear once the routine stops changing behavior and starts preserving appearances. The hard warning is that a written plan can become proof of seriousness while the week quietly stops answering to it. A useful limit keeps this practical. Thinking a written plan controls execution by itself, without weekly process control. The answer is not a bigger speech about discipline. Install a weekly operating routine that turns the plan into reviewed, scheduled, socially supported action. When that happens, process control, Making Sure Things Get Done, Weekly Plans becomes a working standard instead of language in a plan.

In Installing Process Control, process control has to leave proof before the week closes.

Process control also protects morale. When the review happens every week, misses are smaller and less mysterious. The team can ask what changed, what slipped, and who needs help before the cycle is in danger. That is why Don't Go It Alone matters: support arrives while the work can still be recovered.
